Maybe the simplest and most standard is to play Qd6 or Qd8+. In K+Q vs K, the technique is to bring the queen to a knight's move away from the enemy king, then mimic the king's moves to squeeze it to the edge. Here the black king is already on the edge (d1). It seems the most forcing moves are Qd8+ and Qd6. Qd8+ is a check, which might be more forcing in practice because it limits black's replies (black must move out of check). After Qd8+, black has 4 replies: c1, c2, e1, e2. (d2 covered). We saw that c1 leads to Qd1#, c2 leads to Qd3+ Kc1 Qd1#, e2 leads to Qd3+ Kf2 or Ke1... and e1 leads to Qd1+ Kf2... So Qd8+ has the same lines as Qd6 for c2 and e2, but for c1 and e1: in Qd6, c1 is mate in 2 (Qd1#), e1 is not mate in 2 (Qd1+ Kf2). In Qd8+, c1 is still mate in 2? Wait, after Qd8+ Kc1, Qd1# is mate. But is Qd1# legal? Qd8-d1 is along d-file, yes. And we checked it's mate. So Qd8+ Kc1 leads to mate in 2. But Qd8+ Ke1 leads to Qd1+ Kf2. So black's best defense is to play Ke1 or Ke2 (which can lead to Kf2). In Qd6, black's best defense is also Ke1 or Ke2 (leading to Kf2). So both are very similar.

However, Qd6 has a slight advantage: it doesn't force black to move out of check, so black might blunder with Kc1 and get mated in 2. In Qd8+, black might also blunder with Kc1 and get mated. But in Qd6, black has 4 moves, two of which (c1, e1) are on the back rank, and c1 loses immediately. In Qd8+, black has 4 moves, c1 loses immediately, e1 doesn't. So maybe Qd6 is slightly better because it gives black an extra losing option? No, in Qd6, e1 doesn't lose immediately either. Both give c1 as a losing blunder. In Qd8+, c1 is also a losing blunder. So similar.

But there's a difference: in Qd6, black is not in check, so they have the option to move to c2 or e2 as well. In Qd8+, they also have those options. So identical sets of moves: c1, c2, e1, e2. Wait, in Qd6, black also has d2? No, d2 is attacked by Qd6. So black has c1, c2, e1, e2. In Qd8+, black has c1, c2, e1, e2 (d2 attacked). So the exact same set of legal moves! Qd6 and Qd8+ both attack d2, and both leave c1, c2, e1, e2. The only difference is that Qd8+ is a check, so black is in check. But the set of legal moves is identical! Because from d1, when in check from d8, the king can move to any square not attacked, which are c1, c2, e1, e2. From d6, without check, the king can also move to those same squares. So the position after the move is functionally the same in terms of black's options, except in one case black is in check and must move, in the other it's just their turn. But the set of legal moves is identical. Therefore, the resulting positions are exactly the same: white queen on d8 or d6, black king on one of c1, c2, e1, e2. The follow-ups will be very similar. However, the difference is the queen's position: on d8 vs d6.

If queen is on d8 and black plays Ke1, we have Qd1+ Kf2. Queen is on d1.
If queen is on d6 and black plays Ke1, we have Qd1+ Kf2. Queen is on d1. Same.
If black plays Kc2, from d8 we have Qd3+ Kc1 Qd1#. From d6 we have Qd3+ Kc1 Qd1#. Same.
If black plays Ke2, from d8 we have Qd3+ Ke1/Kf2. From d6 we have Qd3+ Ke1/Kf2. Same.
If black plays Kc1, from d8 Qd1#. From d6 Qd1#. Same.

So Qd6 and Qd8+ lead to identical subsequent positions! The only difference is that Qd8+ is a check, which might be considered more forcing in terms of chess etiquette, but the outcome is the same. However, Qd8+ forces black to move, whereas Qd6 leaves black to move anyway. In terms of the game tree, they are literally the same after the first move, because the position after 1. Qd6 and black's move (c1, c2, e1, e2) is: white queen on d6, black king on the square. After 1. Qd8+ and black's move, the position is: white queen on d8, black king on the square. The subsequent moves for white are different because queen is on d8 vs d6. Wait, I said they are the same but they are not! In Qd6 line, after Kc1, we play Qd1# and queen moves from d6 to d1. In Qd8+ line, after Kc1, we play Qd1# and queen moves from d8 to d1. Both result in Qd1#. The intermediate position is different, but the mate is the same. For other replies:
- Kc2: from d6, we play Qd3+ (d6-d3). From d8, we play Qd3+ (d8-d3). Same.
- Ke2: from d6, Qd3+; from d8, Qd3+. Same.
- Ke1: from d6, Qd1+; from d8, Qd1+. Same.

So in all cases, the second white move is identical! Because d8 and d6 both can move to d3 and d1. So the two moves are completely equivalent in terms of the resulting lines. The only difference is whether it's a check or not on the first move. But since black has to move anyway, and the set of legal moves is identical, it's literally the same game tree.

Therefore, both Qd6 and Qd8+ are optimal and equivalent.

Let's think about the standard algorithm for checkmate with queen and king. We want to force the black king to the edge, then bring our king in opposition, and deliver mate with queen. Here black king is already on the back rank (row 1), which is an edge. Our king is on c5. We can use the queen to cut off the king's escape to the 2nd rank and gradually squeeze.

One common method: place the queen a knight's move away from the king to restrict its movement, then bring the king. For king on e1, a knight's move would be d3, f3, c2, g2. We don't have those moves directly, but we can get there. For example, Qh3? That's not a knight's move. Qe5 is not a knight's move.
